# Fixed Points of Projective Transformations and Intersections of Conics

## Linear Hypothesis of Cross Ratio

In the definition of cross ratio, we did not make use of the additive structure on $\mathbb{C}$, i.e. we viewed $\mathbb{C}^\times$ as a multiplicative group where square roots can be taken. We also defined the $\iota$ function satisfying $\iota(A,B;C,D)=(A,C;B,D)$.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
A complex projective plane is said to be linear if the cross ratio is linear, namely, the cross ratio takes value in $\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ and additionally satisfies the following: for any collinear points $A,B,C,D$,

(1) If $B\neq A$, $B\neq C$, then $(A,B;C,B)=0$.

(2) If $A\neq B$, $A\neq C$, then $(A,B;C,A)=\infty$.

(3) $(A,B;C,D)+(A,C;B,D)=1$.

(4) If three of $A,B,C,D$ coincide, then $(A,B;C,D)$ is undefined.

In the following, a complex projective plane is assumed to be linear.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
In Appendix A, we proved that $\mathcal{P}$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{P}_F$ for some field $F$ such that $F^\times\simeq \mathbb{C}^\times$ as groups. Moreover, if $\mathcal{P}$ satisfies the linear hypothesis $\iota(x)=1-x$, then $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{P}_\mathbb{C}$ are isomorphic. This suggests that we may call a complex projective plane without the linear hypothesis a "pseudo-complex projective plane".
:::

Most assertions are provable without the linear hypothesis, but some problems are not easy to deal with. For instance, a projective transformation has at most three non-collinear fixed points (otherwise it is the identity), but showing the existence of a fixed point is essentially solving a cubic equation in $\mathbb{C}$, which is not easy with the multiplicative structure on $\mathbb{C}^\times$ alone.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
Suppose that $F$ satisfies $F^\times\simeq \mathbb{C}^\times$, then for a given prime $p$, there are $p$ $p$-th roots of unity, i.e. there are $p$ solutions to the equation $x^p=1$, so $F$ is not of characteristic $p$ (otherwise the only solution of $0=x^p-1=(x-1)^p$ is $x=1$, which has multiplicity $p$). We conclude that $F$ is of characteristic $0$. Assuming the axiom of choice (Zorn's lemma), we may prove that the algebraic closure of $F$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{C}$, so we may embed $\mathcal{P}_F$ into $\mathcal{P}_\mathbb{C}$. This is another way to force the linear hypothesis, but some points may not be in the original set of points $\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}^2(F)$.
:::

Fixing a reference triangle $ABC$ and reference point $P$, Ceva theorem gives a way to represent the location of a point with a $3$-tuple. However, when the point is on the three sides of $ABC$, the value of the cross ratios may be $\infty$. To deal with this, we can make the coordinate homogeneous. In the following, we introduce a coordinate system that is similar to the classical barycentric coordinates.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Given four points $A,B,C,P$ (no three are collinear), then for any point $X$, consider the values
$$
x_A=A(B,C;P,X),\, x_B=B(C,A;P,X),\, x_C=C(A,B;P,X)
$$
By Ceva theorem, the product of these values is $1$. It follows that there exists a $3$-tuple $(u,v,w)\neq (0,0,0)$ of complex numbers such that 
$$
v/w=x_A, \,w/u=x_B, \,u/v=x_C
$$
Conversely, given a $3$-tuple $(u,v,w)\neq (0,0,0)$ of complex numbers, there exists a unique point $X$ such that
$$
x_A=v/w,\, x_B=w/u,\, x_C=u/v
$$
Note that $(u,v,w)$ and $(cu,cv,cw)$ represent the same point, so this point is denoted $(u:v:w)$. This coordinate system is called the $P$-coordinate with respect to $ABC$. We may think of each point in $\mathbb{P}$ as a one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{C}^3$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
The classical barycentric coordinates are the case where $P$ is the centroid.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
The point $(1:0:0)$ satisfies $x_B=0$, $x_C=\infty$, which is $BA\cap CA=A$. Similarly, $(0:1:0)$, $(0:0:1)$ represent $B$, $C$, respectively. On the other hand, $(0:v_0:w_0)$ represents the point on $BC$ such that $A(B,C;P,X)=v_0/w_0$.
:::

We investigate the relations of points on the same line. The points on line $BC$ satisfy $u=0$. For each point on the line through $A$ and $(0:v_0:w_0)$, the value $x_A$ is fixed, i.e. the points satisfy
$$
v_0w-w_0v=0
$$
In these two cases, lines are represented by a linear equation, i.e. a two-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{C}^3$. For a general line, the linear hypothesis must be added so that it is also represented by a linear equation (this is why I call it the linear hypothesis).

:::{#thm-baryline}
A line is a two-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{C}^3$, which is generated by two points on it.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let a line $\ell$ intersect $BC, CA,AB$ at
$$
D=(0:v_A:w_A),\, E=(u_B:0:w_B), \,F=(u_C:v_C:0)
$$
From Menelaus theorem, $v_Aw_Bu_C+w_Au_Bv_C=0$, so the points $D$, $E$, $F$ satisfy the equation
$$
w_Bv_Cu-w_Bu_Cv-u_Bv_Cw=0
$$
We aim to show that all points on $\ell$ satisfy this equation. By @thm-collinear, $X$ lies on $EF$ if and only if 
$$
B(C,F;E,X)=C(B,F;E,X)=1-C(B,E;F,X)
$$
That is,
$$\dfrac{u_Bw}{w_Bu}= B(C,A;E,P)\cdot B(C,A;P,X)=1-C(B,A;F,P)\cdot C(B,A;P,X)=1-\dfrac{u_Cv}{v_Cu}$$
which simplifies to $w_Bv_Cu-w_Bu_Cv-u_Bv_Cw=0$. This is a two-dimensional subspace.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Three points are collinear if and only if the determinant of the matrix formed by the three points is $0$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
We may use a column vector $\mathbf{x}_0=(u_0\quad v_0\quad w_0)^t$ to represent the point $(u_0:v_0:w_0)$ in $\mathbb{P}$. On the other hand, lines in $\mathbb{L}$ are two-dimensional subspaces, but dually, we may use a row vector $\mathbf{L}=(\alpha\quad\beta\quad\gamma)$ to represent the equation $\alpha u+\beta v+\gamma w=0$. In this way, the point $\mathbf{x}_0$ is on the line $\mathbf{L}$ if and only if $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}_0=0$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Let $X_0=(u_0:v_0:w_0)$. The tripolar $\ell$ of $X_0$ intersects the three sides at
$$D=(0:-v_0:w_0),\,E=(u_0:0:-w_0),\,F=(-u_0:v_0:0)$$
so the equation of $\ell$ is $v_0w_0u+w_0u_0v+u_0v_0w=0$. In other words, the tripolar of $\mathbf{x}_0=(u_0\quad v_0\quad w_0)^t$ is $\mathbf{L}=(v_0w_0\quad w_0u_0\quad u_0v_0)$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $3$. From the equation of the tripolar, $P$ is always on the tripolar of $P$ in $\mathcal{P}_F$.
:::

## Fixed Points of Projective Transformations

A projective transformation $\rho:\mathbb{P}\to \mathbb{P}$ is a function that preserves collinearity and cross ratio. Given a projective transformation $\rho$, $P$ is said to be a fixed point of $\rho$ if $\rho(P)=P$; $\ell$ is said to be a fixed line of $\rho$ if $\rho(\ell)=\ell$.

Elements in $\mathbb{P}$ are represented by column vectors $\mathbf{x}=(u\quad v\quad w )^t$. We aim to show that the action of a complex $3\times 3$ invertible matrix $\mathbf{P}\in \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{C})$ (taking $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{x}$) is a projective transformation. One-dimensional subspaces (resp. two-dimensional subspaces) are sent to one-dimensional subspaces (resp. two-dimensional subspaces) by $\mathbf{P}$, so $\mathbf{P}$ is a transformation on $\mathbb{P}$ that preserves collinearity.

To prove that the transformation $\mathbf{P}$ preserves cross ratio, let $X=\mathbf{x}=(u:v:w)$ be a point varying on line $\ell$, and let $\mathbf{P}$ map the points $A,B,C,X$ to $A',B',C',X'$. Define $X_1=(0:v:w)$ to be the intersection of $AX$ and $BC$, and set
$$X_1'=A'X'\cap B'C'=\mathbf{P}(X_1),\,X_2=AX_1'\cap BC$$
The maps $X\mapsto X_1$ and $X_2\mapsto X_1'\mapsto  X'$ are projective, so it suffices to show that $X_1\mapsto X_2$ is a projective map on line $BC$.

In the following, lowercase boldface denotes the column vector of the corresponding point. Note that 
$$
\mathbf{x_2}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\0&0&1 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{x_1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\0&0&1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p_{11}&p_{12}&p_{13}\\ p_{21}&p_{22}&p_{23}\\p_{31}&p_{32}&p_{33} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\v\\w \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\p_{22} v+p_{23}w\\p_{32}v+p_{33}w \end{pmatrix}
$$
so it suffices to show that the action of the $2\times 2$ submatrix $\mathbf{P}_2$ in the bottom-right corner of $\mathbf{P}$ on the line $BC$ is projective.

The point $Y=(v\quad w)^t$ denotes the point $(0:v:w)$ on $BC$. Recall that we are working under $P$-coordinates. Suppose that $AP\cap BC=P_a$, then $v/w=(B,C;P_a,Y)$. Consider the action of the following invertible matrices $\mathbf{P}_2$ on $BC$:

(1) $\mathbf{P}_2=(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{smallmatrix})$: $\mathbf{P}_2$ is the involution $(B,C)$, $(P_a,P_a)$.

(2) $\mathbf{P}_2=(\begin{smallmatrix}c&0\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix})$, $c\in\mathbb{C}^\times$: let $Z\in BC$ such that $c=(B,C;Y,Z)$, then $\mathbf{P}_2$ maps $Y$ to $Z$.

(3) $\mathbf{P}_2=(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&1\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix})$: let $Z\in BC$ such that $(B,C;P_a,Y)=(B,P_a;C,Z)$, then $\mathbf{P}_2$ maps $Y$ to $Z$.

Since the actions of the three types of matrices are projective, and they generate all $2\times 2$ invertible matrices, the action of any invertible matrix $\mathbf{P}_2$ on $BC$ is projective. This shows that $\mathbf{P}$ is a projective transformation. (We omitted the case where $\mathbf{P}_2$ is not invertible. In this case, $B'C'$ passes through $A$. Suppose that $A,B,C$ lie on $B'C',C'A',A'B'$, respectively, then the previous argument works for the inverse $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ of $\mathbf{P}$.) 

:::{#thm-proj-linear}
A function $\rho:\mathbb{P}\to \mathbb{P}$ is a projective transformation if and only if $\rho$ is an invertible linear transformation on $\mathbb{C}^3$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
It suffices to show that a projective transformation $\rho$ is a $3\times 3$ invertible matrix $\mathbf{P}\in\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{C})$. Consider the $P$-coordinate with respect to $ABC$, let $\rho(A)=(u_A:v_A:w_A)$, and label the coordinates of $\rho(B),\rho(C),\rho(P)$ similarly. Since $\rho(A),\rho(B),\rho(C)$ are not collinear, there exists $(a\quad b\quad c)^t\in\mathbb{C}^3$ such that
$$
\begin{pmatrix}u_A&u_B&u_C\\ v_A&v_B&v_C\\w_A&w_B&w_C\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a\\ b\\c\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}u_P\\ v_P\\w_P\end{pmatrix}
$$
Set
$$
\mathbf{P}=\begin{pmatrix}au_A&bu_B&cu_C\\ av_A&bv_B&cv_C\\aw_A&bw_B&cw_C\end{pmatrix}
$$
Since the coordinate of $P$ is $(1:1:1)$, we see that $\mathbf{P}$ is the projective transformation $\rho$ by plugging in $A,B,C,P$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Since $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}=0\iff \mathbf{L}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{x}=0$, the action of the projective transformation $\mathbf{x}\mapsto \mathbf{P}\mathbf{x}$ on $\mathbb{L}$ is $\mathbf{L}\mapsto \mathbf{L}\mathbf{P}^{-1}$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
A dual transformation $\mathfrak{p}$ is of the form $\mathbf{x}\mapsto \mathbf{x}^t\mathbf{Q}$, so $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}=\{\mathbf{x}\mid \mathbf{x}^t\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}=0\}$ is a conic. Expanding, $\mathbb{P}_\mathfrak{p}$ is of the form 
$$
\{a_1u^2+a_2v^2+a_3w^2+a_4vw+a_5wu+a_6uv=0\}
$$
In particular, we also call conics "quadratic curves".
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
The action of a dual transformation $\mathfrak{p}:\mathbf{x}\mapsto \mathbf{x}^t\mathbf{Q}$ on $\mathbb{L}$ is given by $\mathbf{L}\mapsto \mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{L}^t$, so $\mathfrak{p}^2:\mathbf{x}\mapsto \mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{Q}^t\mathbf{x}$. This shows that $\mathbf{Q}$ is a symmetric matrix when $\mathfrak{p}$ is a polar transformation (since $\mathbf{Q}^t=\lambda\mathbf{Q}$, $\lambda^2=1$, and taking the determinant gives $\lambda^3=1$).
:::

To study the fixed points of projective transformations, it suffices to study the eigenvectors of the corresponding matrices.

:::{#thm-proj-fixed-point}
Any projective transformation $\rho$ has a fixed point.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
The eigenvectors of $\rho=\mathbf{P}$ (i.e. the vectors $\mathbf{x}$ such that $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{x}=\lambda\mathbf{x}$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^\times$) are the fixed points of $\rho$.
:::

To find $\lambda$, i.e. $\mathbf{P}-\lambda\mathbf{I}_3$ is not invertible, we solve for the cubic equation $\det(\mathbf{P}-\lambda\mathbf{I}_3)=0$. Since there always exist solutions for cubic equations, such $\lambda$ and $\mathbf{x}$ exist.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
In fact, we do not need the linear hypothesis to show @thm-proj-fixed-point. Suppose that $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{P}_F$ are isomorphic, where $F$ is a field such that $F^\times\simeq \mathbb{C}^\times$ (in which square roots and cube roots can be taken). By the Cardano formula (i.e. radical solution of a cubic equation), solutions for cubic equations must exist.
:::

Now, we classify the fixed point set and fixed line set of $\rho$. The possible fixed point sets are: a point, two points, three (non-collinear) points, a line, a point and a line, and the entire plane. When the fixed point set is either a line or a point and a line, $\rho$ is a perspective transformation.

Suppose that $\rho$ has a single fixed point $P$, but there exist two fixed lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$ through $P$. Let $X_1\in\ell_1$, $X_2\in\ell_2$. We have
$$
(X_1,\rho(\rho(X_1));\rho(X_1),P)=-1=(X_2,\rho(\rho(X_2));\rho(X_2),P)
$$
(from @lem-uniquefixedpoint). This shows that $X_1X_2$, $\rho(X_1)\rho(X_2)$ and $\rho(\rho(X_1))\rho(\rho(X_2))$ are concurrent, and this point is a fixed point of $\rho$, contradiction. We conclude that when the fixed point set consists of a single point $P$, the fixed line set consists of a single line through $P$.

Suppose that $\rho$ has exactly three fixed points $P,Q,R$, then $PQ,QR,RP$ are fixed lines. Suppose that $\rho$ has exactly two fixed points $P,Q$, then from the cases of one fixed point and three fixed points (and the dual), $\rho$ has exactly two fixed lines.

:::{#cor-fixed-point-classification}
The possible fixed point sets are: a point, two points, three (non-collinear) points, a line, a point and a line, and the entire plane.

(1) When the fixed point set consists of a single point $P$, the fixed line set consists of a single line through $P$.

(2) When the fixed point set consists of exactly two points $P,Q$, the fixed line set consists of the line $PQ$ and another line through one of $P,Q$.

(3) When the fixed point set consists of exactly three points $P,Q,R$, the fixed line set consists of lines $PQ,QR,RP$.
 
(4) When the fixed point set is $\mathbb{P}_\ell$, the fixed line set is $\mathbb{L}_P$ where $P\in \ell$ is the perspector.

(5) When the fixed point set is $\{P\}\cup \mathbb{P}_\ell$, the fixed line set is $\{\ell\}\cup\mathbb{L}_P$.

Summing up, the type of the fixed point set and the fixed line set of a projective transformation correspond dually.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
These six types of the fixed point sets of projective transformations correspond to the possible Jordan canonical forms of $3\times 3$ invertible matrices, so all of these six types exist. The duality follows from the fact that $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ share the same type of Jordan form.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Given a conic $\mathcal{C}$ and $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ such that $f$ has exactly one fixed point $P$, then the extension $\rho$ of $f$ has exactly one fixed point $P$, and the fixed line is the tangent line at $P$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Consider the projective transformation $(u:v:w)\mapsto (2u:v+w:w)$. The fixed points are $(1:0:0)$ and $(0:1:0)$.
:::

## Intersections of Conics and Isoconjugations

:::{#lem-conicintersectionexist}
Two conics $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2$ must intersect.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that the two conics do not intersect, consider the fixed point set 
$$
\{X\mid \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(X)=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(X)\}
$$
of the projective transformation $\rho(X)=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(X))$, which is possibly a single point, two points, three points, a line, a point and a line, or the entire plane.

(1) Suppose that $\rho$ is a perspective transformation. Consider an intersection $S$ of the perspectrix and $\mathcal{C}_1$. Note that the polar of $S$ with respect to $\mathcal{C}_2$ passes through $S$, i.e. $S$ is the intersection of the two conics, contradiction.

(2) Suppose that the fixed point set of $\rho$ consists of a single point $P$. The polar $\ell$ of $P$ is a fixed line of $\rho$, so $\ell$ passes through $P$, i.e. $P$ is the intersection of the two conics (and the tangents at $P$ to the two conics coincide), contradiction.

(3) Suppose that the fixed point set of $\rho$ consists of two points $P,Q$. The polars of $P,Q$ are fixed lines, but one of them is $PQ$. Without loss of generality, assume that line $PQ$ is the polar of $Q$, then $Q$ is the intersection of the two conics.

(4) Suppose that the fixed point set of $\rho$ consists of three points $P,Q,R$. The fixed line set is the three sides of triangle $PQR$, so the polar of $P$ is $QR$ (otherwise the conics intersect at $P$). Similarly, the triangle $PQR$ is self-conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$. Let $PQR$ be the reference triangle. From @cor-diagonalconic, we regard $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}$ and $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}$ as sets collecting the fixed points of collinear isoconjugations. The function $\varphi=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}\cap\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}$ is an isoconjugation on $PQR$, i.e. $\varphi:X\mapsto \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(X)\cap\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(X)$. From @lem-isoconjugatefix, $\varphi$ has $4$ fixed points, which are the intersections of $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$.

We conclude that two conics must intersect.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
We revisit the case (4) of the proof of @lem-conicintersectionexist, i.e. when the fixed points of $\rho$ are exactly $P,Q,R$. In this case, the polar of $P$ must be $QR$ (even if the two conics intersect). Suppose not, we assume that the polar of $P$ is $PR$, then the polar of $R$ is $PQ$, and the polar of $Q$ is $QR$. This shows that $\mathcal{C}_1,\,\mathcal{C}_2$ are tangent at points $P,Q$. Take $S\in PQ$, then $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(S)=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(S)$ passes through $R$ and the harmonic conjugate of $S$ with respect to $P|Q$, which is a contradiction. We conclude that in case (4), the two conics must intersect at $4$ points.
:::

As in case (4), we can generalize the concept of isoconjugations to isoconjugations with respect to two conics.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Define the (point) isoconjugation with respect to the two conics $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ as
$$
\psi(X)=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(X)\cap \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(X)
$$
Suppose that $P$ satisfies $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(P)= \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(P)$ (i.e. the fixed points of $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}\circ\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}$), then $\psi(P)$ is undefined. Note that when $\psi(X)$ and $\psi(\psi(X))$ are defined, $\psi(\psi(X))=X$.
:::

:::{#lem-conicisoconjugatelocus}
Let $\psi$ be the (point) isoconjugation with respect to the two conics $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$, and $\psi$ is not defined at finitely many points. Suppose that $\ell$ is a line such that $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(\ell)\neq \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(\ell)$.

(1) If $\ell$ does not pass through any undefined point of $\psi$, then $\psi(\ell)$ is a conic.

(2) If $\ell$ passes through an undefined point $P$ of $\psi$, then $\psi(\ell)$ is a line through $P$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
For $X\in \ell$, the map $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(X)\mapsto X\mapsto \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(X)$ is projective. By Steiner conic, the locus of $\psi(X)=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(X)\cap \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(X)$ is a line or conic, and the locus is a conic if and only if $\ell$ does not pass through any undefined point of $\psi$. This proves (1). Now assume that $\ell$ passes through an undefined point $P$ of $\psi$, then $\psi(\ell)$ is a line $m$.

i. Suppose that the undefined points are the three points $P,Q,R$. Since $\psi$ is an isoconjugation on $PQR$, $m$ passes through $P$.

ii. Suppose that the undefined points are the two points $P,Q$, and the polar of $Q$ is $PQ$. Let $\ell$ intersect the polar of $P$ at $X$, then $\psi(X)=P$ (note that $\psi(X)$ is defined), so $m$ passes through $P$.

iii. Suppose that the undefined points are the two points $P,Q$, and the polar of $P$ is $PQ$. Since $\psi(m)=\ell$ is a line, $m$ passes through $P$ or $Q$. From ii, if $m$ passes through $Q$, then $\ell$ passes through $Q$, contradiction. We see that $m$ passes through $P$.

iv. Suppose that there is only one undefined point $P$. Since $\psi(m)$ is a line, $m$ passes through $P$.

This proves (2).
:::

:::{#thm-intersectmulti}
If we use the following way to define the multiplicity of intersections, then two conics $\mathcal{C}_1,\,\mathcal{C}_2$ always intersect at $4$ points. Let the isoconjugation be $\psi(X)=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(X)\cap \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(X)$. We consider the set of points where $\psi$ is undefined.

(1) If the set consists of exactly one point, then there are two distinct intersections of the conics, one of which is a tangency point. Define the multiplicity of the tangency point to be $3$.

(2) If the set consists of exactly two points, then there are three distinct intersections of the conics, one of which is a tangency point. Define the multiplicity of the tangency point to be $2$.

(3) If the set consists of exactly three points, then there are four distinct intersections of the conics.

(4) If the set is an entire line, then there is a unique intersection of the conics, which is also a tangency point. Define the multiplicity of this intersection to be $4$.

(5) If the set is the union of a point and an entire line, then there are two distinct intersections, both of which are tangency points. Define the multiplicity of both intersections to be $2$.

If an intersection is not a tangency point, it is said to be of multiplicity $1$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\rho=\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}\circ\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}$. The fixed points of $\rho$ are the undefined points of $\psi$.

Suppose that $\rho$ has a single fixed point $P$. The polar $\ell$ of $P$ passes through $P$, so the two conics are tangent at $P$. By @lem-conicisoconjugatelocus, the involution $f:\mathbb{L}_P\to \mathbb{L}_P,\,m\mapsto \psi(m)$ has two fixed lines $\ell$ and $m_0$, and $m_0$ intersects both conics again at $X_0$. Note that $X_0$ is the only intersection of the two conics other than $P$, and $X_0$ is not a tangency point. This proves (1).

Suppose that $\rho$ has exactly two fixed points $P,Q$, the fixed lines are $PQ,\,\ell$ such that $P\in \ell$. The polar of $P,Q$ are $PQ,\ell$, respectively, and the two conics are tangent to $PQ$ at $P$. The involution $f:\mathbb{L}_P\to \mathbb{L}_P,\,m\mapsto \psi(m)$ has two fixed lines $m_1$ and $m_2$, and $m_i$ intersects both conics again at $X_i$ ($i=1,2$). This proves (2).

Suppose that $\rho$ has exactly three fixed points. We studied this case in @lem-conicintersectionexist, which proves (3).

Suppose that $\rho$ is a perspective transformation such that the perspector $P$ is on the perspectrix $\ell$. In this case, $\ell$ is tangent to the two conics at $P$. Suppose that the two conics intersect at $Q\neq P$, then there exists a point $X$ on $\ell$ such that $XQ$ intersects $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2$ at distinct points $Y_1,Y_2$, respectively. The lines $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_i}(X)$ ($i=1,2$) pass through the harmonic conjugate of $X$ with respect to $Q|Y_i$, so $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_1}(X)\neq \mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(X)$, which is a contradiction, i.e. there are no other intersections. This proves (4).

Suppose that $\rho$ is a perspective transformation such that the perspector $P$ is not on the perspectrix $\ell$. In this case, the pole of $\ell$ is $P$, and both $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2$ intersect $\ell$ at two distinct points $Q,\, R$. Moreover, $PQ,PR$ are tangent to both conics. This proves (5).
:::

## Three Conic Theorem

:::{#lem-restintersect}
Let two conics $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ intersect at points $A,B,C,D$ (not necessarily distinct). Let $m_A$ be a line through $A$, which intersects $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ again at $A_1,A_2$; let $m_B$ be a line through $B$, which intersects $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ again at $B_1,B_2$. For all $m_A\in\mathbb{L}_A,m_B\in \mathbb{L}_B$, we have
$$
A_1B_1\cap A_2B_2\in CD
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Fix $m_B$ (such that $B_1\neq B_2$) and vary $m_A$, then the map
$$\mathbb{L}_{B_1}\to \mathbb{L}_{B_2}:B_1A_1\mapsto B_2A_2$$
is projective. Moreover, when $m_A=AB$, $B_1A_1=B_2A_2$, so the locus of $B_1A_1\cap B_2A_2$ is a line $\ell$.

Let $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}_1$ intersect at $C',D'$. When $A_1=C'$, $A_2$ has to be $C'$. We see that the two intersections of $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}_1$ are the same as those of $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$. Suppose that there is an intersection $E$ of $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ that is not on $AB$. Taking $m_A=AE$, $E$ is on $\ell$, i.e. $\ell\cup AB$ contains all intersections of $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$. Since there are only four intersections, there are finitely many possibilities of $\ell$. That means, as $m_B$ varies, we obtain the same $\ell$.

We aim to show that $\ell=CD$, i.e. $\{A,B,C,D\}=\{A,B,C',D'\}$ (counted with multiplicity). Suppose that $P$ is counted at least twice in $\{A,B,C',D'\}$. When $A=B=P$ or $C'=D'=P$, the two conics are tangent at $P$; when $B=D'=P$, $\ell$ passes through $B$, so we fix $m_B$ to be the tangent of $B$ to $\mathcal{C}_1$ (suppose that $B\neq B_2$), then as $m_A$ varies, the locus of $BA_1\cap B_2A_2$ passes through $B$, which is a contradiction, so $B=B_2$ and the two conics are tangent at $P$.

This shows that if $P$ is counted exactly once in $\{A,B,C,D\}$, then it is also counted once in $\{A,B,C',D'\}$, and the two sets are equal if multiplicity is not counted. Considering the $5$ possibilities of the intersections of two conics, to prove that the two sets are equal (counted with multiplicity), it suffices to verify the case where the conics are tangent at two distinct points.

Suppose that $A=C,\,B=D$. Taking $m_A$ to be the tangent at $A$, we see that $A\in \ell$, and similarly $\ell=AB=CD$. Suppose that $A=B,\,C=D$. In this case the two conics are tangent at $A,C$ (note that $C\in\ell$). Taking $m_A,\,m_B$ such that $(AB,AC;m_A,m_B)=-1$, we see that
$$
(A,C;A_i,B_i)_{\mathcal{C}_i}=-1,\,i=1,2
$$
This shows that $A_1B_1\cap A_2B_2$ is the intersection of the tangents at $A$ and $C$, i.e. $\ell=CD$ is the tangent at $C$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
@lem-restintersect suggests that the definition of the multiplicities in @thm-intersectmulti is reasonable.
:::

From @lem-restintersect we may prove the three conic theorem.

:::{#thm-threeconic}
## three conic theorem
Suppose that the conics $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2,\mathcal{C}_3$ all pass through points $A,B$. Let $\mathcal{C}_2,\mathcal{C}_3$ intersect again at $A_1,B_1$; $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_3$ intersect again at $A_2,B_2$; $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2$ intersect again at $A_3,B_3$. The lines $A_1B_1,A_2B_2,A_3B_3$ are concurrent.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $AA_3,BB_3$ intersect $\mathcal{C}_3$ again at $X,Y$, respectively. Apply @lem-restintersect to $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_3$ and the lines $AA_3,BB_3$, then $A_2B_2,A_3B_3,XY$ are concurrent. Similarly, $A_1B_1,A_2B_2,A_3B_3$ are concurrent on $XY$.
:::

@lem-restintersect is the degenerate version of the three conic theorem.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Let the circles $\omega_1,\omega_2$ intersect at $A,B\neq \infty_{\pm}$. Given $P_1,Q_1$ on $\omega_1$ and $P_2,Q_2$ on $\omega_2$, $P_1Q_1\parallel P_2Q_2$ if and only if the points $A,B,P_1,Q_1,P_2,Q_2$ lie on the same (possibly degenerate) conic.
:::

The intersections of two circles refer to the two intersections other than the circular points at infinity.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
The **radical axis** of two circles is the line connecting their two intersections.
:::

:::{#cor-radicalcenter}
Let $\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3$ be circles. Let the radical axis of $\omega_2,\omega_3$ be $\ell_{23}$, and define $\ell_{31},\ell_{12}$ similarly. The lines $\ell_{23},\ell_{31}, \ell_{12}$ are concurrent, and the concurrency point is called the **radical center** of the three circles.
:::
